item.title: Shared and context-dependent cortico-striatal-cerebellar organization of temporal prediction
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Pinho, A. L., Koranteng-Addo, V., Alsibaie, A., Patel, N., Diedrichsen, J., Grahn, J. A.
Temporal prediction is thought to draw on two subcortical structures: the basal ganglia for the periodic beat, and the cerebellum for the aperiodic interval. Lesion, imaging and electrophysiological studies converge on this division, yet each tests it within a single modality and task, leaving its generality unknown. We developed a battery of timing tasks for multi-task fMRI, densely sampling 31 non-clinical adults in every combination of temporal structure, sensory modality and task. Encoding engaged the same cortico-striatal-cerebellar architecture throughout. Within it, the dorsal striatum was uniquely selective for the production task. Pooled across tasks, it responded more to auditory beat than interval sequences, whereas the cerebellum did not distinguish them. Yet, removing regularity did not lower that response: the preference is for the beat, not for predictability. Temporal prediction therefore draws on a shared architecture whose striatal node is context-dependent: tuned to periodic time, and to time turned into action.

item.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Bao Pham
arXiv:2611.26797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

item.title: Surface Cues Over Structure: Probing LLM Behavior on Brain Connectivity Graphs
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Prapti Roy, Khaled Mohammed Saifuddin
arXiv:2611.26913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) provides a noninvasive view of functional interactions across the brain, which can be represented as connectivity graphs for neurological disease analysis. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being paired with such representations, yet it remains unclear whether they genuinely reason over the underlying connectivity or simply respond to surface-level cues that may trigger learned priors. We probe this question through a controlled study of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) diagnosis from resting-state functional connectivity, isolating one factor at a time to determine what drives an LLM's predictions on brain connectivity graphs. Across six models, from small open-weight LLMs to a proprietary one, the same pattern holds: the results provide little evidence that predictions are consistently grounded in subject-specific connectivity. Brain region names, numeric formatting, and prompt framing shift what a model predicts without improving how well it separates ADHD subjects from Controls; perturbing the graph changes predictions no more for clinically meaningful regions than for random ones; and the models' own justifications contradict the values they cite, inconsistently interpreting the connectivity evidence provided to them. Across every probe, predictions follow the model's built-in class bias and the surface form of the prompt rather than the subject's connectivity, calling into question a premise underlying current LLM brain integration work. Our code is available at https://github.com/Roy025/ADHD-code.

item.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wang, Q., Guo, Y., Nie, W., Yang, Q., Zhang, S., Luo, C., Zhang, Y., Zuo, X.-N.
Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

item.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Andrea Gregor de Varda, Ferdinando D'Elia, Greta Tuckute, Evelina Fedorenko, Meenakshi Khosla
arXiv:2611.26920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

item.title: From Gist to Verbatim: The Controllable Path of One Image Through a Diffusion Prior
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Luca Saglietti, Luca Giammanco, Marc Mezard, Chiara Plizzari, Luca Biggio
arXiv:2611.27875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern generative models are typically studied for their ability to generalize, while memorization is treated as a failure mode. We invert this perspective and ask how a generative model can recall a single datum. We frame memorization as a control problem: a learned conditioning signal steers a frozen diffusion model toward a target image, and we follow the formation of this memory throughout training. Before converging to exact reproduction (verbatim), memory passes through a regime of abstraction: samples preserve the target's semantic content (gist) while remaining diverse in appearance, leaving predictable detail to the generative prior. This semantic organization emerges despite the absence of labels, captions, or any explicit semantic objective. In the abstraction regime, the learned memory approaches ordinary text conditioning and supports editing, one-shot recognition, and retrieval more effectively than in the near-perfect reconstruction regime. These results suggest that memorization can serve as a probe of the relevance structure encoded by a generative model: what must be stored about a datum, what can be reconstructed from prior knowledge, and how learned memories interpolate between reconstructive recall and literal data storage.

item.title: EmPraWS - Indirect response retrieval across different modalities
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: SocArXiv
Vanessa Wolf et al.
This experiment studies the possible role of stimulus – stimulus association in transferring an existing stimulus-response association for a given stimulus to the other associated stimulus which was not previously linked with the response. The focus will be specifically on how the response can be transferred across different modalities. This is established by initially pairing two stimuli – one visual and one auditory stimulus together (step 1). Then, the visual stimulus is paired with a response and the pattern between stimulus and response is learnt (step 2). Following this the matched associated stimulus which is in another modality, namely an auditory stimulus is introduced and its ability to retrieve the response of the visual stimulus is tested (step 3). Evidence for indirect retrieval of a response via a stimulus-stimulus association refers to sensory preconditioning.

item.title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Anirudh Atmakuru, Tanya Goyal
arXiv:2611.26863v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reasoning domains have shaped the post-training recipes of frontier models even though they are trained and deployed in domains beyond math and code. In this paper, we study the consequences of directly adopting reasoning-centric training recipes, e.g., the use of outcome-based rewards for reinforcement learning (RL), injection of "cognitive" behaviors such as proposing and backtracking from hypotheses in reasoning chains, etc., for knowledge tasks. We hypothesize that these decisions, while useful for reasoning, inadvertently encourage models to memorize hallucinations they themselves generate in their long reasoning chains when trained on knowledge tasks. To study this, we train models with standard post-training, extract their self-generated hallucinations during RL, and track memorization throughout the rest of training. Our experiments on six open models across two model families and two architectures confirm our hypothesis. We find that models' recall of hallucinations reinforced during training increases by 4.83% on average, compared to just 0.17% for self-hallucinations that receive no training signal. In fact, models even memorize false facts that they immediately retract in their reasoning; a backtracking template inherited from reasoning-centric training that has no benefit for knowledge recall. Furthermore, we find that memorization is strongest on the hardest training questions, and rewarding a hallucination makes the model less likely to abstain from it later (by 7.23% on average). Overall, our work identifies and systematically studies a previously unexamined pathway through which models learn hallucinations during training.

item.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Weikang Qiu, Zheng Huang, Tinglin Huang, Yujun Yan, Rex Ying
arXiv:2611.27029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.

item.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Temudo, A., Nicolas, J., King, B. R., Albouy, G.
Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

item.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu
arXiv:2611.26902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.

item.title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Xiaoyu Luo, Chengxing Lin, Jiaxin Huang, Jiale Liu, Jingyu Guo, Sirui Chen, Aolin Li, Shaoli Huang, Cheng-zhong Xu, Hui Kong
arXiv:2611.27219v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

item.title: Growing a Neural Network in Breadth, Depth, and Time
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Eivinas Butkus, Kedar Garz\'on Gupta, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte
arXiv:2605.25174v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Brains and AI systems alike must achieve their goals with limited space, time, energy, and data. Here we focus on space and time, defining differentiable costs for breadth (channels), depth (layers), and time (recurrent steps) in a recurrent convolutional network. We optimize these costs jointly with task error via backpropagation. Pricing each resource differently, we grow a diverse set of computational graphs through optimization. We find that breadth, depth, and time can be traded off against each other at a given level of accuracy. Networks grow with task complexity and, when allowed to adaptively allocate time per input, take more recurrent steps if inputs are occluded. The time the model spends on each image also correlates with human reaction times, despite no training on human data. Our work takes a step toward a normative account of how spatial and temporal resource costs jointly shape neural architectures in brains and machines.

item.title: The language network responds stronger to connected than to unconnected sentences
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Paliga, F., Javed, Z., Unnerstall, M., Haj Mohamad, S. H. M., Neef, A., Kube, J. M. V., Malinova, V., Abboud, T., Dechent, P., Riedel, C. H., Neef, N. E.
Purpose: Reliable functional mapping of the language network and preoperative assessment of language lateralization are essential for safe and effective craniotomy in patients with lesions in language-eloquent brain regions, yet existing fMRI language paradigms are often time-consuming and place substantial cognitive and economic demands on patients and diagnostic services. Methods: We therefore tested ecologically valid German stimulus sets designed to optimize measurement efficiency. Forty-three healthy participants (mean age = 38 years, range = 20 - 64; 24 women) were scanned on a 3T MRI while reading or listening to 4-, 8-, and 12-word sentences and pseudoword lists or texts, each followed by a decision task. Sentences were selected from German literary classics and text passages from general-interest science magazines and matched across conditions for lexical and structural properties. Results: Region-of-interest analyses in subject-specific, functionally defined language-sensitive regions showed robust activation of the left-hemispheric language network across modalities. Within participants, texts elicited significantly larger effect sizes than sentences, and longer sentences generally produced stronger responses than shorter ones. Task manipulations expected to increase cognitive demand (short 4-word sentences with frequent probes, coherent texts requiring deeper semantic integration) did not enhance responses in the domain-general multiple demand network, indicating that executive-control activity did not overshadow language-selective activation, whereas substantial overlap between default mode and language-sensitive regions in the left temporal lobe was consistent with relatively automatic processing of connected language. Conclusions: These findings indicate that ecologically valid sentence- and text-based paradigms can provide efficient, language-specific fMRI protocols for preoperative diagnostics and individualized presurgical planning in patients with lesions near language-eloquent cortex.

item.title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv AI
Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Jinli Ou, Yuhua Zheng, Jianqiang Huang
arXiv:2611.26972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.

item.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Stanislav, B. T., Mangnus, M., Stehr, D., Lewis, A. G., Hagoort, P., Basnakova, J., Stolk, A.
Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.

item.title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Hiroshi Higashi, Keigo Sugihara, Yuichi Tanaka
arXiv:2611.26949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.

item.title: Pathogenesis of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): Two Conflicting Prediction Errors, Homeostatic Set Points, and Norepinephrine
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: SocArXiv
Hongwei Zhu
As a person with OCD, I have conducted self-experiments over the past decade guided by Exposure and Response Prevention therapy, while meticulously documenting my emotional and behavioral responses to each intervention. 1) I have found that the Prediction Error (PE) theory is the theoretical model that best aligns with human emotional and behavioral responses. The human brain mainly engages in six types of cognitive activities: perceptual inference, cognitive reasoning, downregulating homeostatic set points, planning motor sequences, planning compensatory motor sequences, and shifting attention. Among these, the first five are major mechanisms for eliminating prediction errors, whereas the last only reduces the generation of prediction errors and cannot eliminate already formed prediction errors. These cognitive activities constitute the neural basis of cognitive flexibility. 2) the brain may contain a neural circuit induced by cognitive reasoning. The basolateral amygdala and nucleus accumbens may be regions where prediction errors are computed, although they differ significantly. The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC, particularly the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC)) might mediate the expression of the homeostatic set point, and the Anterior Hippocampus -sgACC pathway mediates the retrieval of the homeostatic set point. Phasic firing of dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area–vmPFC pathway may mediate the real-time upregulation of homeostatic set points induced by reward cues. The rostral anterior cingulate cortex (rACC), anterior insula, periaqueductal gray , and von Economo neurons may mediate the downregulation of homeostatic set points. The neural mechanism of mindfulness involves the real-time downregulation of homeostatic set points mediated by the rACC. The dorsal anterior cingulate cortex may mediate the planning and storage of compensatory motor sequences. In addition, there may exist a neural circuit induced by actual stimuli, Activation of the limbic thalamic nuclei may encode the homeostatic set point of this circuit. 3) The cerebellum may mediate the expression of body homeostatic set points related to performing actions to complete their functions. 4) The initial onset of OCD is triggered by the emergence of two mutually conflicting prediction errors (PEs) that cannot be effectively eliminated through the six cognitive activities mentioned above. A high level of norepinephrine is also an important factor in the onset and maintenance of OCD. The "perfectionism" exhibited by OCD patients results from the disruption of the real-time downregulation of homeostatic set points mediated by the rACC caused by norepinephrine. Therapeutic approaches based on these six cognitive activities are highly consistent with normal human cognitive patterns, are extremely effective in restoring patients' cognitive flexibility, and will significantly advance the treatment of severe OCD and our understanding of its pathogenesis.

item.title: Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Zunhai Su, Bohan Sun, Xialie Zhuang, Shuibai Zhang, He Xiao, Hui Shen, Jing Xiong, Hengyuan Zhang, Zhongzhu Zhou, Tiantian Zhang, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo
arXiv:2608.12149v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the first systematic study of massive activations (MAs) in layer-interleaved Hybrid linear attention large language models (HLA LLMs), examining their architectural organization, training-time emergence, underlying mechanisms, and functional significance. Across five linear attention architectures, six hybridization configurations, and five input domains, we identify two architecture-aligned morphologies: pre-attention spikes (PAS) immediately before full attention and inter-spike plateaus (ISP) persisting through intervening linear attention layers. Denser full attention increasingly connects PAS through ISP, approaching the persistent MAs of conventional Transformers. This organization also recurs across 12 public checkpoints spanning 1.2B-397B parameters, covering linear attention and state-space hybrids. Controlled pretraining of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids up to 1.3B reveals early emergence and consolidation of both morphologies, alongside asymmetric gating effects. Specifically, full attention output gates strongly attenuate MA magnitudes without eliminating their organization, whereas removing GDN output gates yields modest amplification. Mechanistically, we develop a shared systematic-outlier account: PAS follows a localized write-sink-cancel process, while ISP is consistent with delayed cancellation. Functionally, our interventions show that deleting only the four largest-magnitude PAS coordinates at each full attention input reduces mean downstream accuracy by 21.9%-63.6% relative to normal inference. Moreover, reference-conditioned spike-to-plateau connection consistently improves mean real-world retrieval accuracy, yielding relative gains of 1.1%-12.6% without retraining. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/Massive-Activations-HLA.

item.title: Neural Geometry as a Learning Signal
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Eric Todd, Tal Haklay, Nikhil Prakash, Matthew Finlayson, Michael Hanna, Fenil R. Doshi, Daniel Wurgaft, Thomas McGrath, Owen Lewis, David Bau, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel, Atticus Geiger
arXiv:2611.26832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether the geometric structure of neural representations can provide a sufficient learning signal for improving model behavior without any supervision on model outputs. First, we fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B to answer questions such as "What month is four months after June?" by supervising internal representations of the input month (June = 6) and offset (4), which are encoded with Fourier harmonics. Second, we fine-tune the model to predict line breaks in text wrapped to a fixed width by supervising an internal representation of the number of characters since the preceding newline, which is represented by a low-dimensional helical structure. In both tasks, we supervise a low-dimensional subspace of the residual stream using an idealized target structure, and find that internal geometric supervision achieves similar performance to standard fine-tuning (despite no supervision on outputs). Moreover, we find that simply patching in an ideal geometry is not sufficient to recover fine-tuning performance, and thus demonstrate geometric supervision provides beneficial effects beyond the representations it targets. Together, these findings show how mechanistic understanding of neural geometry can be leveraged to shape the behavior of neural networks.

item.title: Classical visual illusions in vision-language models under an instruction ladder
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Eiji Watanabe
arXiv:2611.27242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often name the "illusory" answer when shown a classical visual illusion, but it is unclear whether that answer comes from the picture or from knowledge about famous figures. We drew 300 new stimuli of 25 classical illusions in three conditions--the illusion, the illusion with its inducing elements reversed, and a control with the inducing elements removed--and asked about each image at eight rungs of an instruction ladder that runs from a false fact, through a neutral question and an instruction to report the physical truth, to telling the model the name of the illusion and finally the true answer. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, with thinking off and on, gave 460,800 answers. When asked for the physical fact, all four settings almost never gave the illusion answer, and they resolved real 10% differences in the same displays. When asked how the picture looks, the illusion answers returned, and they did not vanish after the true answer was stated. Two measures that cancel position preferences and recognition of the figure suggest that much of this depends on the stimulus: among side answers, Sonnet with thinking chose the illusion side in 85% of cases after being told the truth (95% CI 74--96%), with 16 of the 25 illusions showing a stimulus-driven effect. Yet for five figures--the Fraser spiral, Kanizsa triangle, Pinna--Brelstaff rings, Ouchi pattern and, for Haiku, the rotating snakes--the models gave the illusion answer to the control images as well, which suggests that they answered from the figure rather than from the effect. A false fact was mostly followed on control images but not on illusion images. The stimuli, prompts, all responses and the code are released for testing further models; the Python code that draws the stimuli is parametric and can generate new illusion images for other studies with models or human observers.

item.title: Direction and speed selectivity properties for spatio-temporal receptive fields according to the generalized Gaussian derivative model for visual receptive fields
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Tony Lindeberg
arXiv:2511.08101v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper gives an in-depth theoretical analysis of the direction and speed selectivity properties of idealized models of the spatio-temporal receptive fields of simple cells and complex cells, based on the generalized Gaussian derivative model for visual receptive fields. According to this theory, the receptive fields are modelled as velocity-adapted affine Gaussian derivatives for different image velocities and different degrees of elongation. By probing such idealized receptive field models of visual neurons to moving sine waves with different angular frequencies and image velocities, we characterize the computational models to a structurally similar probing method as is used for characterizing the direction and speed selective properties of biological neurons. By comparison to results of neurophysiological measurements of direction and speed selectivity for biological neurons in the primary visual cortex, we find that our theoretical results are consistent with (i) velocity-tuned visual neurons that are sensitive to particular motion directions and speeds, and (ii) different visual neurons having broader vs. sharper direction and speed selective properties. Our theoretical results in combination with results from neurophysiological characterizations of motion-sensitive visual neurons are also consistent with a previously formulated hypothesis that the simple cells in the primary visual cortex ought to be covariant under local Galilean transformations, so as to enable processing of visual stimuli with different motion directions and speeds.
